lead: Verification asks one question: are we building the product right? It compares the SRS, the design and the code against what was written down, and nothing is executed. Validation asks a different question: are we building the right product? It runs the software against the user's real need. Quality assurance prevents defects by shaping the process, while quality control detects defects in the product that already exist. These four labels place every quality activity in a project, so a team knows whether a defect should be caught by a review or by a test, and whether money should go into the process or into more testing.
prereq: You need: the SDLC phases (see Unit 1, Software and Process Models) and the idea of a test case from Chapter 4.1.

sections.h3: Verification: are we building the product right?

blocks.text: Verification compares a work product with the document or standard it must satisfy. Work products are the SRS, the design models, the code and the test plans. A person reads and compares; no code runs. Because nothing executes, verification is called static.

It exists because defects are cheap early and costly late. A wrong sentence in the SRS takes minutes to fix in a review and weeks to fix after release. A two-hour review of a 60-requirement SRS that finds 9 defects usually saves far more than two hours of later testing.
The static techniques, from least to most formal:

items: Desk check: the author rereads their own work against a checklist. Some syllabi call this a deskcheck.
Walkthrough: the author presents the document to two to four colleagues, who ask questions and note problems.
Review: a small team with fixed roles (moderator, author, recorder, reviewers) reads against a checklist and records every defect found.
Inspection: the most formal review, with entry and exit criteria and collected data.

blocks.text: A code review checks one extra thing: that the code follows the team's coding standards (naming, indentation, comment rules, error handling) and matches the design. Review procedure and roles are in Unit 6.

Validation compares the running product with the user's real need. It needs execution, so it is dynamic. Its levels are unit, integration, system and acceptance testing (see Chapter 4.5 and Chapter 4.6).

Why both are needed: a team can verify perfectly — every design matches the SRS, every line matches the design — and still fail, because the SRS itself described the wrong product. Verification catches did we build it as specified; validation catches was the specification right.

The V-model links the two. Every development phase has a matching test level, planned while that phase runs: requirements match acceptance testing, design matches system and integration testing, code matches unit testing. The left arm of the V is verification of each work product; the right arm is validation at that level.

Take the requirement "a user pays a bill in under 30 seconds". Verification checks that the SRS states it, measures it in seconds and makes it testable. Only running the app with real users shows whether they actually manage it.

Quality assurance (QA) is process-oriented and preventive. It builds a way of working that keeps defects out: coding standards, review rules, test policy, training, checklists, process audits and the metrics that show whether the process works. QA acts before the product exists.
Quality control (QC) is product-oriented and detective. It examines an output — a document, a build, a release — for defects already in it. Reviews of deliverables and all testing are QC.

They are not synonyms and not alternatives. QA decides that every code change needs a review before merge and that a build must pass 40 payment tests. QC is the review and the test run on one specific build. When QC finds three failing payment tests, that evidence goes back to QA, which strengthens the weak process step that let the defects in.

spec.aria: Four boxes. Verification lists three reviews finding 9, 6 and 15 defects, 30 in all. Validation shows ten user times as dots against a 30-second line, eight under it and two at 38 and 45 seconds. QA shows 114 of 120 changes reviewed, 95 percent. QC shows 37 of 40 tests passed, 92.5 percent, with a dashed arrow back to QA.

examples.question: A UPI app must let a user pay a ₹250 chai bill in under 30 seconds. Records for one release: (i) a review of the SRS (60 requirements) found 9 defects; (ii) a design review found 6 defects; (iii) a code review of 2400 lines found 15 defects; (iv) 10 users each tried once — 8 finished under 30 s with times 21, 23, 25, 27, 22, 24, 26, 24 s, and 2 took 38 s and 45 s; (v) 114 of 120 code changes were reviewed before merge; (vi) 40 payment tests ran on the release build and 37 passed. Classify each record, then compute the percentage of users meeting the target, the mean time of those users, the review coverage and the test pass rate.
steps: Classify by the question asked. (i), (ii), (iii) read documents and code against the SRS and design, and nothing runs: verification. (iv) runs the product with real users against the 30-second need: validation. (v) is a rule about how work is done before merge: QA. (vi) inspects the built release for defects: QC.
Verification defects caught before any test ran: 9 + 6 + 15 = 30 defects.
Sum of the successful times: 21 + 23 + 25 + 27 + 22 + 24 + 26 + 24 = 192 s. Mean = 192 ÷ 8 = 24.0 s, which is below the 30 s limit.
The two failures at 38 s and 45 s did not meet the need. Validation is not passed, so the 45 s path gets a defect report and the release is not accepted.
Review coverage (QA evidence): 114 × 100 ÷ 120 = 95.0%. Six changes merged without review — an assurance gap to fix in the process.
Test pass rate (QC evidence): 37 × 100 ÷ 40 = 92.5%. The 3 failures are QC findings that go back to QA as process feedback.
examples.answer: Verification: (i)–(iii), 30 defects found without running code. Validation: (iv), 80.0% of users met the 30-second target with mean 24.0 s. QA: (v), 95.0% review coverage. QC: (vi), 92.5% test pass rate.
examples.check:
users_ok = 8
users = 10
times = [21, 23, 25, 27, 22, 24, 26, 24]
print(9 + 6 + 15)
print(users_ok * 100 / users)
print(sum(times) / len(times))
print(114 * 100 / 120)
print(37 * 100 / 40)

traps: Saying testing is the only form of validation. Reviews and inspections also test documents; they are verification.
Saying quality assurance and quality control are synonyms. QA is preventive and process-oriented; QC is detective and product-oriented.
Claiming verification needs the code to run. Verification can be done on paper; validation cannot.
Confusing requirements validation (checking that the SRS states the right need, from Unit 2) with product validation (checking that the running software meets that need).
Writing desk check and deskchecking as two different techniques. They are the same technique, spelled two ways in different syllabi.

quiz.q: Define verification and validation, and give the standard question each answers.
quiz.a: Verification compares a work product (SRS, design, code, test plan) with the document or standard it must satisfy: are we building the product right? Validation compares the running product with the user's real need: are we building the right product? Verification is static; validation is dynamic.

quiz.q: State two preventive QA activities and two detective QC activities.
quiz.a: QA: writing a coding standard and training testers on the automation tool (also review rules, process audits, checklists). QC: reviewing a design document against the SRS and running the payment test suite on a release build.

quiz.q: Explain how a team can pass every verification step and still fail validation.
quiz.a: Verification only checks that each work product matches the one above it: code matches design, design matches SRS. If the SRS itself describes the wrong need, every check still passes because every check agrees with the SRS. Only running the product against the user's real need, i.e. validation, exposes the mismatch.

quiz.q: Classify each as verification, validation, QA or QC: (a) a design review, (b) an acceptance test, (c) a rule that every merge needs one reviewer, (d) regression tests on a new build.
quiz.a: (a) verification — a document compared with the SRS, nothing executed. (b) validation — the running product compared with the user's need. (c) QA — a preventive rule about the process. (d) QC — inspecting a product (the build) for defects.

quiz.q: A review of an 80-requirement SRS finds 12 defects. Later, 9 of 12 users complete a payment task unaided. Compute the defect density per requirement and the task success rate.
quiz.a: Defect density = 12 ÷ 80 = 0.15 defects per requirement. Task success rate = 9 × 100 ÷ 12 = 75.0%. The first number is verification evidence, the second is validation evidence.

quiz.q: A team hires more testers and doubles the test count, but the number of defects reported by customers after release stays the same. What does this tell you about QA and QC in that team?
quiz.a: QC effort rose while escaped defects did not fall, so the product-level check is not the limiting factor. The process is still letting the same class of defect in — for example missing requirements reviews, no coding standards, or no review before merge. QA must change the process (reviews, standards, training) so later testing finds fewer defects, and the escape data should drive which process step is fixed.

quiz.q: In the V-model, why is the acceptance test designed during the requirements phase rather than after coding?
quiz.a: Designing the acceptance test forces the team to state each requirement in measurable, testable form (for example, pay in under 30 seconds), which is verification of the requirement itself. It also fixes the exit criteria before coding starts, so the right arm of the V can be run without rediscovering what the user wanted, and any untestable requirement is caught while it is still cheap to change.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, part of verification has moved into tools: linters, type checkers and static analysers run on every commit, and code review happens in pull requests rather than in meeting rooms. CI pipelines automate the QC side by rerunning the test suite on every build. The QA and QC split survives in standards such as ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 for testing and ISO/IEC 25010 for product quality, and in job titles that now read quality engineer rather than tester. Formal methods and model checking push verification further, proving properties of a design without executing it. Useful search terms: shift-left testing, static analysis, pull request review, process audit.
